name: Doxepin (Silenor, SINEquan)
summary: Sedating tricyclic antidepressant used at very low doses for sleep maintenance and at higher doses for depression and anxiety. Potent antihistamine and anticholinergic with overdose and cardiac risk, and a boxed warning for suicidal thoughts and behaviors in younger patients.
description: Doxepin is a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) that boosts serotonin and norepinephrine while strongly blocking histamine (H1) receptors. In modern psychiatry, it’s used mainly in very low doses for sleep maintenance insomnia, and occasionally as an add-on or later-line option for depression or anxiety when other treatments haven’t worked. At antidepressant doses it carries substantial anticholinergic burden (dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, urinary retention), orthostatic hypotension, and cardiac conduction risks, and overdose can be fatal. Like all antidepressants, doxepin carries a boxed warning about increased suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults. It is not approved for pediatric use.
patient_summary: Doxepin is an older antidepressant that doctors now mostly use in tiny doses to help people stay asleep through the night. In higher doses it can treat depression and anxiety, but because it is quite sedating and has more side effects than newer antidepressants, it’s usually not a first choice. Common issues include dry mouth, constipation, feeling groggy, weight gain, and dizziness when you stand up. Very high doses or overdoses can affect the heart and can be life-threatening. Like all antidepressants, it can temporarily increase suicidal thoughts in some younger people, so close monitoring is important when starting or changing the dose.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Antidepressant, Tricyclic (Tertiary Amine); Histamine H1 Antagonist

linked_conditions.context: Considered a later-line option for treatment-resistant unipolar depression because of side-effect burden and overdose toxicity compared with SSRIs/SNRIs.
Historically used for anxiety, but no longer recommended as first-line due to anticholinergic, cardiac, and overdose risks.
Approved as an adjunct in bipolar depression but can precipitate mania or rapid cycling; avoid without a mood stabilizer and generally not preferred in modern guidelines.
Very low-dose doxepin (3–6 mg) is an FDA-approved option for sleep-maintenance insomnia when behavioral treatments are insufficient.

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to doxepin, dibenzoxepins, or formulation components
Concomitant use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or use within the past 14 days
Use of doxepin within 14 days of stopping an MAOI
Acute recovery phase after myocardial infarction (Canada)
Acute congestive heart failure or severe cardiac conduction disease (Canada)
Pediatric use for depression or insomnia (doxepin is not approved in children; Silenor is approved only in adults)

efficacy_response.comparison_data: Typical target range 50–150 ng/mL; levels above ~300 ng/mL associated with increased toxicity risk.
efficacy_response.patient_text: Blood levels of doxepin and its main metabolite can be measured. Most people respond within a certain range, and very high levels raise the risk of side effects like confusion, heart rhythm changes, and severe sedation.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed orally; high-fat meals significantly increase tablet (Silenor) exposure and delay peak levels by about 3 hours.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Approximately 27% due to extensive first-pass metabolism.
pharmacokinetics.onset: Sleep: first night at hypnotic doses. Mood/anxiety: partial benefit in 1–2 weeks, full effect over 4–6 weeks.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Parent doxepin ~15 hours; active metabolite nordoxepin 31–51 hours.
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Sedative and anticholinergic effects often last into the next day at antidepressant doses.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic via CYP2C19 and CYP2D6 (with minor CYP1A2 and 3A4 contribution) to active metabolite N-desmethyldoxepin (nordoxepin).
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (<3% as unchanged drug or nordoxepin); remainder as metabolites.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Silenor tablets taken with or shortly after a high-fat meal have increased bioavailability and delayed peak, which can worsen next-day sedation; recommended to avoid taking within 3 hours of food.

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: Doxepin is an older, sedating tricyclic antidepressant. In current practice it is used mostly in very low doses for insomnia and only selectively at higher doses for depression or anxiety when safer options fail.
items: Major depressive disorder (unipolar), treatment-resistant: Later-line option when multiple first-line antidepressants have been ineffective or not tolerated; overdose toxicity and side effects limit use.
Anxiety disorders: Historically approved for anxiety, but now rarely used because SSRIs/SNRIs and psychotherapy are safer and better tolerated.

Bipolar depression (adjunct only): Can be used with a mood stabilizer for bipolar depression in selected, closely monitored cases. Not recommended as monotherapy and generally not a guideline-preferred option.
Insomnia with sleep-maintenance difficulty: Very low-dose doxepin (3–6 mg) is FDA-approved to help people who can fall asleep but wake up frequently or too early.
off_label: Chronic insomnia when behavioral therapy alone is insufficient and alternatives are ineffective or poorly tolerated
Sedating adjunct in complex mood or anxiety presentations when other medications have failed (with careful attention to cardiac and anticholinergic risk)

sections.heading: What People Often Feel
sections.intro: Experiences with doxepin depend a lot on the dose: a tiny hypnotic dose feels very different from a full antidepressant dose.

quotes: I still fall asleep on my own, but I’m not waking up over and over all night.
I don’t feel ‘knocked out’ — more like the nighttime awakenings are smoothed out.
If I take it too late, I can feel a bit groggy in the morning.
items.note: At hypnotic doses, antihistamine effects dominate; anticholinergic and cardiac effects are much lower but still possible.

quotes: I was very sleepy and foggy in the morning, even after a full night’s sleep.
It helped my anxiety, but I felt slowed down and heavy all day.
Standing up too fast made me lightheaded.
items.note: Higher doses cause strong antihistamine and anticholinergic effects, leading to sedation, dizziness, and cognitive slowing.

quotes: My mouth felt like cotton; I had to sip water constantly.
I got constipated and needed a stool softener.
My vision was a little blurry, especially up close.
items.note: Dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, and urinary hesitancy are classic tricyclic side effects and are dose-dependent.

quotes: My mood lifted a bit after a couple of weeks, but the side effects were hard to tolerate.
Sleep improved first, then my anxiety felt less sharp.
I had to change to a different antidepressant because of weight gain and brain fog.
items.note: Improvement in mood and anxiety is usually gradual over several weeks. For many people, newer antidepressants provide a better balance of benefits and side effects.

quotes: When I stopped too quickly, I felt dizzy and edgy for a few days.
Tapering slowly made it much easier — I just felt a bit off for a short time.
My sleep got worse again when we stopped, so we had to re-evaluate my plan.
items.note: Abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal-type symptoms (flu-like feelings, sleep disturbance, irritability). A slow taper is preferred.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Doxepin has different timelines for sleep versus mood.
key_points: Sleep (hypnotic doses): Many people notice fewer night-time awakenings from the first or second night.
Depression/anxiety (antidepressant doses): Early changes may appear after 1–2 weeks, with full benefit often taking 4–6 weeks.
Half-life: About 15 hours for doxepin and 31–51 hours for its active metabolite; this means sedative effects can carry into the next day, especially at higher doses.
Steady state: Drug levels stabilize after ~10–14 days of consistent dosing.
Withdrawal: Symptoms (if they occur) usually begin within a few days of abrupt discontinuation and settle over 1–2 weeks; slower tapers reduce this risk.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.metric: Clinical response rather than a single numeric target
sections.text: For sleep-maintenance insomnia, low-dose doxepin has been shown to modestly increase total sleep time and reduce awakenings, with a safety profile similar to placebo at doses ≤6 mg. For depression and anxiety, doxepin is roughly comparable in efficacy to other tricyclic antidepressants, but modern guidelines generally favor SSRIs/SNRIs or other agents because they are safer in overdose and better tolerated. In bipolar depression, antidepressants (including doxepin) are used cautiously and only with a mood stabilizer due to the risk of triggering mania or rapid cycling.
sections.clinical_details: Doxepin’s role has shifted over time. Historically, it was a standard TCA for depression and anxiety. With the advent of SSRIs/SNRIs, its antidepressant use declined due to anticholinergic burden, cardiac conduction risk, and high lethality in overdose. Its strongest modern evidence base is for sleep-maintenance insomnia at 3–6 mg nightly, where antihistaminergic effects improve sleep architecture with relatively low risk, especially compared with benzodiazepines or ‘Z-drugs.’ For major depression, it may still be considered in carefully selected, treatment-resistant cases where other options have failed and cardiac risk can be monitored.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Boxed Warning: Antidepressants, including doxepin, can increase suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults. Doxepin is not approved for use in pediatric patients.
sections.black_box: Monitor all patients starting or changing the dose of doxepin for worsening depression, emergent suicidal thoughts, agitation, or unusual behavior changes—especially in the first few months and after dose increases or decreases. Families and caregivers should be instructed to watch for abrupt mood or behavior shifts and to seek urgent help if they occur.
other: Overdose risk: Tricyclic overdoses are medical emergencies and can be fatal due to dangerous heart rhythm disturbances, seizures, and profound CNS depression.
Cardiac conduction abnormalities: At higher doses or in vulnerable patients, doxepin can prolong PR, QRS, and QT intervals and precipitate serious arrhythmias.
Anticholinergic burden: High risk of dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurry vision, cognitive changes, and delirium, especially in older adults.
Orthostatic hypotension and falls: Blood pressure can drop when standing, increasing the risk of syncope and fractures.
Angle-closure glaucoma and urinary retention: Mydriasis and anticholinergic effects can trigger acute angle-closure glaucoma or worsen urinary obstruction in susceptible patients.
Hyponatremia/SIADH: Rare but possible, especially in older adults or those on diuretics; may present with confusion, headaches, or seizures.
Seizure risk: Tricyclics can lower seizure threshold, particularly in overdose or in patients with underlying risk factors.
Serotonin syndrome: Risk increases when combined with other serotonergic drugs (eg, SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, linezolid, triptans).
Severe respiratory or sleep apnea: Sedative effects can worsen sleep apnea; doxepin is generally avoided in severe cases.
Withdrawal symptoms: Abrupt discontinuation after weeks to months of treatment can cause flu-like symptoms, insomnia, irritability, and other discomforts.
patient_counseling: If you notice new or worse depression, suicidal thoughts, intense anxiety, agitation, or unusual behavior changes, contact your prescriber immediately or seek emergency care.
Never take more than prescribed or use doxepin for self-harm; even a relatively small overdose can be life-threatening.
Call your doctor or go to the ER right away if you develop chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, fainting, or severe dizziness.
Seek urgent eye care if you suddenly develop eye pain, blurred vision, halos around lights, or red, painful eyes.
Avoid alcohol and limit other sedating medications unless specifically cleared by your prescriber—combined sedation can be dangerous.
Do not stop doxepin suddenly unless you are instructed to for safety reasons. Most people should taper slowly to reduce withdrawal symptoms.
Tell your prescriber if you have glaucoma, urinary problems, prostate enlargement, severe constipation, or a history of heart disease before starting.
Keep all medicines, especially tricyclics, locked away from children, teens, and anyone at risk of overdose.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Doxepin’s side-effect profile is dominated by sedation, anticholinergic effects, weight gain, and cardiovascular changes. Risk increases with dose and in older or medically fragile patients.
plain_language_list: Sleepiness and next-day grogginess, especially at higher doses or when taken with food or other sedatives
Dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, and trouble urinating (classic anticholinergic effects)
Dizziness or feeling faint when standing up (orthostatic hypotension), which can lead to falls
Weight gain and increased appetite over time
Sexual side effects such as reduced libido
Rare but serious heart rhythm changes or conduction problems, particularly in overdose

common.incidence: Up to ~15–20% or higher at antidepressant doses; lower but still present at hypnotic doses
common.patient_note: Expect to feel sleepy; for insomnia treatment this is part of the goal. If you feel heavily sedated or unsafe to drive or work, let your prescriber know—your dose or timing may need adjustment.
Sipping water, sugar-free gum, and good oral hygiene can help. Severe dryness can increase dental problems; inform your dentist and prescriber if this is persistent.
Increase fiber and fluids, and consider a stool softener if recommended. Sudden inability to pass stool, abdominal pain, or vomiting needs urgent evaluation.

common.incidence: A few percent at typical doses, higher in older adults and at higher doses
common.patient_note: Stand up slowly, especially at night. If you faint, fall, or feel your heart racing, contact your prescriber promptly.
Often temporary and related to anticholinergic effects. Report persistent or painful visual changes immediately.

common.incidence: ≈2–5% in trials; can be higher with long-term treatment
common.patient_note: Track your weight and appetite. Lifestyle changes and alternative medications may be needed if weight gain becomes problematic.

serious: Suicidal thoughts or behavior, particularly in children, adolescents, and young adults at the start of treatment or after dose changes.
Serious cardiac arrhythmias: palpitations, wide QRS, QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, syncope, or sudden cardiac arrest—especially with overdose or pre-existing heart disease.
Seizures, particularly in overdose or in those with risk factors.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma: sudden eye pain, blurred vision, halos, red eye, nausea/vomiting.
Severe urinary retention: painful inability to pass urine, abdominal distention, or worsening of prostate symptoms.
Hyponatremia/SIADH: confusion, headache, weakness, seizures, or worsening falls in older adults.
Serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic agents: agitation, tremor, sweating, fever, confusion, stiff muscles, and unstable vital signs.
Severe allergic or hypersensitivity reactions: facial or tongue swelling, difficulty breathing, hives, or rash.
Blood disorders (rare): low white blood cells or platelets, with symptoms like frequent infections, bruising, or bleeding.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Doxepin is metabolized by CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 and has both serotonergic and cardiac effects. Many interactions are clinically important.

items.risk: High risk of severe serotonin syndrome, hypertensive crisis, and CNS toxicity.
items.action: Contraindicated. Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting doxepin, and 14 days between stopping doxepin and starting an MAOI.

items.with: Other serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, other TCAs, tramadol, linezolid, triptans, St. John’s wort)
items.risk: Increased risk of serotonin syndrome; overlapping adverse effects (eg, GI upset, agitation, sleep disturbance).
items.action: Use with caution, preferably avoid combinations with multiple serotonergic agents. Monitor for agitation, tremor, sweating, and confusion.

items.with: QT-prolonging drugs (certain antipsychotics, macrolide antibiotics, methadone, some antiarrhythmics)
items.risk: Additive QT prolongation and higher risk of ventricular arrhythmias, including torsades de pointes.
items.action: Avoid when possible. If combination is necessary, obtain baseline and follow-up ECGs and correct low potassium or magnesium.

items.with: CNS depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines, other sleep medications)
items.risk: Enhanced sedation, cognitive impairment, risk of respiratory depression, and falls.
items.action: Minimize concurrent use. If unavoidable, use lowest effective doses and counsel patients not to drive or use heavy machinery.

items.with: Strong CYP2D6 or CYP2C19 inhibitors (eg, fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, fluvoxamine, some PPIs)
items.risk: Increased doxepin exposure, with more pronounced sedation, anticholinergic effects, and toxicity.
items.action: Consider lower starting doses and slower titration. Monitor for side effects. In known poor metabolizers, dose reductions are recommended.

items.with: Medications with strong anticholinergic properties (eg, some antipsychotics, antihistamines, bladder antispasmodics)
items.risk: Additive risk of dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, confusion, and delirium—especially in older adults.
items.action: Avoid stacking multiple anticholinergics when possible. If needed, monitor bowel function, urinary function, and cognition closely.

items.risk: Antidepressants can enhance bleeding risk, particularly when combined with aspirin, NSAIDs, or anticoagulants, though the risk appears lower with doxepin than with SSRIs.
items.action: Use caution; monitor for bruising, nosebleeds, GI bleeding, or anemia. Maintain gastroprotection if at high GI-bleed risk.

sections.heading: Stopping Doxepin Safely
sections.text: Stopping doxepin abruptly can cause a withdrawal or discontinuation syndrome, especially after longer-term use or higher doses.
key_points: Typical taper: Reduce the dose gradually over 2–4 weeks after at least 4 weeks of treatment. For long-term or high-dose use, tapering over several months may be needed.
Short courses (2–3 weeks): Many people can taper over 1–2 weeks; treatment under 2 weeks may not require a taper, but a brief step-down is often still more comfortable.
Withdrawal symptoms: Flu-like feelings, sleep disturbance, irritability, anxiety, ‘rebound’ insomnia, nausea, headache, and occasionally movement symptoms or mood swings.
If severe symptoms appear: Return to the previous tolerated dose and taper more slowly.
Bipolar disorder: When stopping an antidepressant in bipolar depression, monitor for relapse, mood switching, or rapid cycling.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Doxepin is used at very different dose ranges depending on the target: tiny doses for sleep versus much higher doses for depression and anxiety.

adult.insomnia_hypnotic: Tablet (Silenor): 3–6 mg by mouth once nightly within 30 minutes of bedtime; maximum 6 mg/night. Do not take within 3 hours of a meal. Some clinicians may use a 10 mg capsule off-label when tablets are not available, with caution for next-day sedation.
adult.depression_treatment_resistant: Capsule/oral concentrate: Typically start 25–75 mg once at bedtime. Increase by 25–50 mg every ≥3 days based on response and tolerability. Usual total daily dose 100–300 mg given once at bedtime or split into 2–3 doses. Maximum single dose generally 150 mg.
adult.anxiety: Similar to depression dosing: 25–75 mg at bedtime initially, titrating up to 100–300 mg/day in divided or bedtime dosing. Modern guidelines rarely recommend doxepin for anxiety due to safety concerns.
adult.bipolar_depression_adjunct: Use similar antidepressant dosing but only in combination with a mood stabilizer and with careful monitoring for mania or rapid cycling. Often avoided in favor of other options.
adult.switching_to_from_maoi: Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting doxepin, and at least 14 days between stopping doxepin and starting an MAOI.

elderly.insomnia: Start with 3 mg (Silenor) nightly; increase to 6 mg only if clearly needed. Doses above 6 mg/day are considered potentially inappropriate in older adults due to anticholinergic and fall risk.
elderly.depression_anxiety: In general, avoid high-dose tricyclics in older adults. If used, consider starting at about half the usual adult dose and titrate very cautiously with ECG and fall-risk monitoring.

hepatic.note: Doxepin is hepatically metabolized; exposure can be higher in liver impairment.
hepatic.recommendation: For capsules/oral concentrate, many experts reduce both starting and maintenance doses by ~50% and titrate carefully. For Silenor, manufacturers recommend starting at 3 mg nightly in liver impairment.

renal.note: Less than 3% of doxepin is excreted unchanged in urine.
renal.recommendation: No routine dose adjustment is required for kidney impairment, including dialysis; however, clinical monitoring is still important.

pediatric.note: Doxepin is not approved for pediatric depression or insomnia. Small pediatric doses for insomnia or depression appear in literature but should only be used by specialists due to safety and suicidality concerns.

sections.simple_explanation: For sleep, doxepin is used in tiny doses (3–6 mg) mainly to keep you asleep. For depression or anxiety, doses are much higher (100–300 mg/day), which brings more side effects and cardiac risk. Older adults and people with liver problems need lower and slower dosing.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Doxepin can be used in pregnancy or breastfeeding only after carefully weighing risks and benefits and considering alternatives. It poses particular concerns in older adults and those with heart disease, glaucoma, urinary retention, or liver disease.
sections.pregnancy: Data on doxepin itself are limited, but overall tricyclic antidepressants have not shown a major increase in birth defects as a group. Untreated depression, anxiety, or bipolar disorder during pregnancy also carries significant risks to both parent and baby. Doxepin is not a first-line choice in pregnancy; if a TCA is needed, clinicians often prefer agents with more data. Patients who are stable and doing well on doxepin before pregnancy may sometimes remain on it if the benefits clearly outweigh the risks, using the lowest effective dose and careful monitoring.
sections.lactation: Doxepin and its active metabolite enter breast milk. Case reports describe infants with marked sedation, poor feeding, and hypotonia that improved after breastfeeding stopped, while another report describes no apparent harm. Because infants—especially newborns—may be more vulnerable to sedation and respiratory depression, doxepin is generally not a first-choice antidepressant in breastfeeding, and many guidelines prefer other agents. If a parent continues doxepin while nursing, the infant should be closely monitored for sedation, poor feeding, inadequate weight gain, and developmental progress.
sections.pediatrics: Doxepin is not approved for use in children for depression or insomnia. TCAs carry a boxed warning for increased suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children and adolescents, and modern guidelines favor SSRIs and psychosocial interventions for pediatric mood and anxiety disorders.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults are particularly sensitive to sedation, orthostatic hypotension, anticholinergic effects, cognitive impairment, falls, fractures, and hyponatremia. Beers Criteria flag doxepin at doses >6 mg/day as potentially inappropriate. If used at all, it should be at the lowest dose, with careful monitoring and strong consideration of safer alternatives.
sections.hepatic: Liver impairment decreases clearance of doxepin and increases active drug levels. Lower doses, slower titration, and careful monitoring for sedation, confusion, and toxicity are required.
sections.renal: Kidney impairment has minimal impact on doxepin elimination, but clinical vigilance is still needed, particularly in complex or medically ill patients.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mood and suicidality: Worsening depression, emergent suicidal thoughts, agitation, or behavior changes, especially in the first 1–2 months or during dose adjustments.
ECG, heart rate, and blood pressure: Particularly in older adults, people with cardiac disease, or those on QT-prolonging or interacting medications.
Electrolytes: Baseline and as clinically indicated, especially potassium and magnesium when there is arrhythmia risk or diuretic use.
Weight, BMI, and metabolic parameters: Track weight gain and appetite changes over time.
Anticholinergic burden: Ask about constipation, urinary retention, dry mouth, blurry vision, and cognitive changes.
Signs of hyponatremia: Fatigue, confusion, falls, or seizures—especially in older adults or those on diuretics.
Liver function tests: Baseline and as needed in patients with liver disease or on higher doses long term.
Sleep quality: In insomnia treatment, track sleep-maintenance benefit versus next-day sedation or cognitive impairment.
Adherence and overdose risk: Reassess safety regularly in patients with self-harm history or high access to medications.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Doxepin comes in several oral forms, with hypnotic (Silenor) tablets dosed very differently from higher-dose capsules and solutions.
items: Capsules (US, Canada): 10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 75 mg, 100 mg, 150 mg – used for antidepressant/anxiolytic dosing.
Oral concentrate (US): 10 mg/mL – must be diluted with water, milk, or certain juices (not carbonated beverages) before use.
Tablets (Silenor, US/Canada): 3 mg and 6 mg – specifically designed and labeled for sleep-maintenance insomnia; do not take within 3 hours of a meal.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text: Doxepin increases serotonin and norepinephrine in the brain by blocking their reuptake into nerve cells, which can improve mood and anxiety over time. It also strongly blocks histamine H1 receptors, which makes it very sedating and useful for maintaining sleep at very low doses. In addition, it has anticholinergic and alpha-adrenergic blocking properties, which contribute to side effects like dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, urinary retention, and low blood pressure when standing.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In contemporary psychiatry, doxepin’s primary niche is as a low-dose hypnotic for sleep-maintenance insomnia when behavioral interventions alone aren’t sufficient and alternatives are not tolerated or effective. For depression and anxiety, it is no longer a first-line agent because of its anticholinergic load, overdose toxicity, and cardiac risks; SSRIs, SNRIs, and other newer agents are favored. In bipolar depression, tricyclics (including doxepin) are generally avoided or used only in specific, treatment-resistant cases in combination with mood stabilizers due to the risk of mood destabilization. Doxepin requires careful patient selection, shared decision-making, and close monitoring when used at antidepressant doses.

seo.title: Doxepin (Silenor, SINEquan): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects, Sleep & Suicide Risk
seo.description: Doxepin for insomnia, depression, and anxiety: how low-dose Silenor works for sleep maintenance, typical antidepressant doses, side effects (sedation, anticholinergic, cardiac), overdose risk, suicidal thoughts warning, pregnancy and breastfeeding considerations, and safe tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA and Health Canada prescribing information, APA and CANMAT guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature on tricyclic antidepressants, insomnia treatments, and perinatal psychiatry.

faqs.q: What is doxepin used for today?
faqs.a: Doxepin is an older tricyclic antidepressant. Nowadays it is used mainly in very low doses (3–6 mg) as Silenor to help people stay asleep through the night. Higher-dose capsules or liquid can still be used for treatment-resistant depression or anxiety, but newer antidepressants are usually preferred because they are safer in overdose and have fewer side effects.

faqs.q: How does doxepin help with sleep?
faqs.a: At low doses, doxepin strongly blocks histamine H1 receptors in the brain. Histamine is one of the chemicals that helps keep you awake. By dampening histamine signaling, doxepin makes it easier to stay asleep and reduces nighttime awakenings, without acting like a classic sedative-hypnotic or benzodiazepine. It should be taken 30 minutes before bed and not within 3 hours of a meal.

faqs.q: How long does doxepin take to work for depression or anxiety?
faqs.a: For mood and anxiety symptoms, doxepin typically takes 1–2 weeks to start making a noticeable difference, with full benefit often taking 4–6 weeks at a stable dose. Sleep often improves sooner. If there is no meaningful change after an adequate trial at a therapeutic dose, your prescriber may recommend a dose adjustment or a different treatment.

Doxepin is not considered addictive in the same way as benzodiazepines or opioids, and it is not a controlled substance. However, your body can get used to it, and stopping suddenly—especially after higher doses or long-term use—can cause withdrawal-type symptoms such as anxiety, flu-like feelings, and rebound insomnia. That’s why it should usually be tapered slowly under medical supervision.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking doxepin?
faqs.a: It’s best to avoid alcohol while on doxepin. Both alcohol and doxepin depress the central nervous system, so combining them can greatly increase sedation, slow reaction time, impair judgment, and raise the risk of falls, accidents, or breathing problems—especially at higher doses or in older adults.

faqs.q: Is doxepin safe for older adults?
faqs.a: Doxepin must be used very cautiously in older adults. Doses above 6 mg/day are considered potentially inappropriate because they can cause confusion, falls, urinary retention, constipation, and heart rhythm changes. When used at all, doctors usually stick to low doses (3–6 mg for sleep), monitor closely, and strongly consider safer alternatives.

faqs.q: Can I take doxepin if I have glaucoma or trouble urinating?
faqs.a: Doxepin can worsen narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention due to its strong anticholinergic effects. If you have glaucoma, a history of urinary retention, or significant prostate problems, you should inform your prescriber before starting doxepin. In many cases it will be avoided, or used only with extreme caution and specialist input.

faqs.q: How do I stop taking doxepin safely?
faqs.a: Do not stop doxepin abruptly unless your prescriber advises you to for safety reasons. Most people benefit from a gradual taper over several weeks, reducing the dose stepwise to minimize withdrawal symptoms such as insomnia, flu-like feelings, anxiety, and mood swings. If you feel very unwell when tapering, your prescriber may temporarily increase the dose again and slow down the taper.

Like all antidepressants, doxepin carries a boxed warning that it can increase suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults during the first months of treatment or after dose changes. The overall risk is small, but it is serious. Anyone starting or changing a doxepin dose should be monitored closely for worsening mood, agitation, or new suicidal thoughts, and urgent help should be sought if these occur.
